rites.desc: Followers of the spider goddess Biliku, Bilikuists maintain a combative relationship with their Gods. Biliku herself is said to directly enact vengeance on her followers with monsoons if they destroy her creations and fail to live in harmony with the world she created. The pantheon includes Biliku and her husband, their children, and countless human Ancestors.
rites.name: Bilikuism

rites.desc: Pūlugaists believe that the world was forged by the lizard god Pūluga, before he grew frustrated with humanity and struck it with a great flood. Only two men and two women survived, and Pūluga helped them to recreate the world, humanity rediscovering fire and Pūluga recreating all natural things. Followers maintain a complex, often combative, relationship with Pūluga. Acts which spark Pūluga's wrath spawn natural disasters, but can be subverted with proper sacrifice.
rites.name: Pūlugaism

rites.desc: Gyur Bön or 'transformed Bön' is a spiritual tradition founded by Shenchen Luga that evolved alongside the Buddhist traditions of Tibet, growing out of the esoteric movements that predominated the Era of Fragmentation.
rites.name: Gyur Bön

rites.desc: Khyarwé Bön or 'erring Bön' is the indigenous faith of the Tibetan region. Exact beliefs varied from place to place but ritualism, sacrificial offerings, and animistic beliefs were common among believers.
rites.name: Khyarwé Bön

rites.desc: The path to enlightenment goes through personal experience, reflection and reasoning. Gautama Buddha found his own path to Nirvana, and the only way of finding a similar way, is to experience, learn and study ones own existence.
rites.name: Theravada

rites.desc: Release from Samsara is not merely something done individually, but an experience that is shared among sentient beings. Achieving buddhahood is one step on the long path for all sentient beings to be released into Nirvana, and that is the virtuous goal of Samsara.
rites.name: Mahayana

rites.desc: Avatamsaka Buddhists regard the Flower Garland Sutra as the supreme source of truth, which speaks of an infinity of worlds, of entire universes contained within a single mote of dust.
rites.name: Avatamsaka

rites.desc: Dhyana Buddhism strongly emphasizes deep and profound meditation as the only viable path to enlightenment — one can achieve true understanding only through inward reflection and contemplation, and not through the study of scriptures.
rites.name: Dhyana

rites.desc: The Lotus Sutra is revered and venerated before all others in Pundarika Buddhism, which emphasizes mantras and complex rituals and originated in a mixture of tantric and esoteric elements transmitted to China along the Silk Road.
rites.name: Pundarika

rites.desc: Sukhavati, or Pure Land Buddhism, teaches that traditional routes to enlightenment are no longer possible. However, by invoking the compassion of Amitābha by reciting his name, one may be reborn in his Pure Land after death, whether monk or layman.
rites.name: Sukhavati

rites.desc: Adherents of Vinaya Buddhism hold themselves and each other to rigorous moral and ethical standards, for self-discipline is the foundation necessary for the pursuit of profound wisdom.
rites.name: Vinaya

rites.desc: Yogacara Buddhists question that which others simply take for granted throughout their lives, treating the material world as nothing more than a manifestation of their own consciousnesses.
rites.name: Yogacara

rites.desc: The age of Sakyamuni Buddha is over and Maitreya Buddha has descended to the world, or so believe those who exalt and embrace Maitreya as their prophesied savior. It is only through the destruction of the old order that the world can be saved.
rites.name: Maitreya

rites.desc: The motivation towards buddhahood is crucially important, and true enlightenment can only be achieved when sought for the benefit of all sentient beings. All beings are born with an enlightened mind, but it is obscured by existence. Practicing seeing the truth of the world and the universe therefore unlocks one's innate enlightenment.
rites.name: Vajrayana

rites.desc: Acharya, a derivative of Vajrayana Buddhism, crystallized in the ninth century with the intermingling and integration of Chinese rites and Tibetan tantric practices, resulting in a uniquely regionalized manifestation of Buddhist practices and worship.
rites.name: Acharya

rites.desc: The Ari faith combines elements from tantric Buddhism, spirit worship, traditional Nāga worship as well as Hinduism. Ari worshipers are considered to be Buddhists, although their practices are perceived as somewhat unorthodox.
rites.name: Ari

rites.desc: Mantrayanan Buddhists augment their understanding of the profound and accelerate their spiritual journey with an array of esoteric rituals and mystical implements.
rites.name: Mantrayana

rites.desc: Buddhism in Tibet is known as Nangchos, or the Dharma of the Insiders. Within the Tibetan Empire, Vajrayana and Mahayana beliefs and practices syncretized with traditional Tibetan beliefs, practices, and deities, with varying schools also competing with each other for temporal control.
rites.name: Nangchos

rites.desc: The Roman rite is the liturgical tradition of the Church of Rome, shaped by Latin theology, juridical authority, and an emphasis on sacramental discipline, clerical hierarchy, and institutional unity.
rites.name: Roman Rite

rites.desc: Proper to the Archdiocese of Milan since the days of its great bishop St. Ambrose, the Ambrosian Rite maintains its own liturgy and chant, and a theological tradition that prizes the thought of St. Augustine of Hippo.
rites.name: Ambrosian Rite

rites.desc: The liturgical tradition of the Lombard south, centered on Benevento and the great abbey of Montecassino. Its distinctive chant and observances set it apart from the Roman practice, which eyes the rite with growing suspicion.
rites.name: Beneventan Rite

rites.desc: A form of Christianity that developed under the reign of the Carolingian dynasty, characterized by its emphasis on monasticism and missionary work.
rites.name: Carolingian Christianity

rites.desc: The Georgian Rite represents the Christian traditions of Georgia, characterized by a distinct liturgy, ecclesiastical heritage, and strong ties to Eastern Orthodox theology and practice.
rites.name: Georgian Rite

rites.desc: The Patriarchate of Constantinople is one of the most significant centers of Eastern Orthodox Christianity, known for its rich theological traditions and historical influence. Greek Rite stems directly from the patriarchy.
rites.name: Greek Rite

rites.desc: A rural church that drifted away from Roman Catholic orthodoxy some centuries ago, Insular Rite has lost many of its once-distinctive features at the insistence of its mother-church. It yet retains a greater emphasis on penance and monasticism, and incorporates many traditional Celtic marriage customs foreign to wider Christendom.
rites.name: Insularism

rites.desc: A descendant of the early Iberian rites, the Mozarabic Rite retains a measure of independence from Rome after centuries of Islamic rule. Long cohabitation with other faiths has bred a tolerance of difference the stricter sects lack.
rites.name: Mozarabism

rites.desc: Brought to the Slavic folk by Cyril and Methodius, this rite incorporates elements of Byzantine liturgy adapted to Slavic languages and culture via the Glagolitic alphabet.
rites.name: Slavic Rite

rites.desc: Tracing its origins to Saint Mark the Evangelist, the Coptic Church is famous for both being the birthplace of Christian monasticism as well as maintaining a long tradition of the promotion of education and philosophy.
rites.name: Coptic

rites.desc: The Patriarchate of Antioch is one of the oldest Christian communities, founded by St. Peter and St. Paul the Apostles. Its West Syriac tradition, called 'Jacobite' after Jacob Baradaeus who reorganized the church, upholds the Miaphysite teaching and the ancient liturgy of St. James.
rites.name: Antiochian Rite

rites.desc: Centered in Ethiopia's highlands and rooted in Aksum's legacy, this ancient Christian tradition differs from other Alexandrian churches by maintaining a broader scriptural canon, strong monastic traditions, and a covenant shaped by Solomonic royal heritage.
rites.name: Ge'ez

rites.desc: Founded by the Apostles Bartholomew and Thaddeus, the Armenian Apostolic Church rapidly gained followers in the region and shepherded the Kingdom of Armenia into becoming the first state ever to adopt Christianity as its official religion.
rites.name: Apostolic

rites.desc: The Conversos originated when Jewish communities were forcibly converted to Christianity. Though they have embraced their new faith, they still remember their old traditions and are sympathetic towards those who still follow them.
rites.name: Conversos

rites.desc: An austere dualist rite that holds the material world to be the work of an evil demiurge. Its perfecti take vows of poverty and chastity, reject the sacraments of the established church, and refuse military service in the name of God.
rites.name: Catharism

rites.desc: A rite of barefoot mendicant preachers who insist that the laity may preach scripture, that the institutional church has no exclusive claim on grace, and that Christians should hold no property or take up arms.
rites.name: Waldensianism

rites.desc: A vernacular reform rite that rejects ornate ritual, transubstantiation, the cult of relics, and a wealthy clergy. The Bible is read in the common tongue and every believer is held to be a priest in their own right.
rites.name: Lollardy

rites.desc: A Bohemian reform rite that demands the chalice for the laity, scripture in the vernacular, and an end to clerical wealth and the sale of indulgences. Its preachers draw heavily on Wycliffite arguments and the burning conviction that Rome has strayed from the apostolic path.
rites.name: Hussitism

rites.desc: An apocalyptic rite that reads history in three ages: Father, Son, and a coming Age of the Holy Spirit that will dissolve the institutional Church and raise up a new contemplative order. Its adherents wander in apostolic poverty, preach in the marketplaces, and gaze with bright eyes at the imminent end of the world.
rites.name: Joachimism

rites.desc: A revival of the old eastern aniconist movement, condemning the veneration of images as a creeping idolatry and demanding that icons be stripped from churches and homes alike.
rites.name: Iconoclasm

rites.desc: A Slavic dualist rite that traces its roots to the priest Bogomil. Its preachers travel barefoot, reject hierarchy, refuse to bear arms, and teach that Satan is the maker of the visible world.
rites.name: Bogomilism

rites.desc: A martially-oriented dualist rite born in Asia Minor. Scornful of icons and established religious hierarchies, its followers prize the unmediated reading of Paul's epistles, and are quite willing to take up arms in defense of their purity.
rites.name: Paulicianism

rites.desc: In teaching that Jesus Christ has two natures, one divine and one human, Nestorianism has been declared as heretical by most Christian faiths. Despite this, its unique outlook has garnered followers in places as far east as China, India, and even Mongolia.
rites.name: Nestorianism

rites.desc: An esoteric, ascetic rite which regards ceaseless prayer as the only sacrament of any worth. For once the demon dwelling within a believer is expelled, no carnal act can ever defile that believer again.
rites.name: Messalianism

rites.desc: The Adamites claim to have recaptured Adam and Eve's original state of innocence by shedding their clothes. Groups of Adamites often live in a state of absolute lawlessness, claiming that due to this innocence their actions can be neither good nor evil.
rites.name: Adamitism

rites.desc: Long forgotten by Catholic and Orthodox alike, the Krstjani of the Bosnian highlands are more permissive than their better-known compatriots, but lack formal structure. Retaining many archaic elements of Christianity, they are often treated scornfully by coreligionists, if remembered at all.
rites.name: Krstjani

rites.desc: A Christological rite from Iberia teaching that Christ, in his humanity, was the adopted and not the natural Son of God — a doctrine the Carolingian church condemned as Crypto-Nestorianism.
rites.name: Adoptionism

rites.desc: Daoxue Confucianism rejects esoteric influences and traditions and instead places a strong emphasis on secular rationalism and rigorous intellectual inquiry.
rites.name: Daoxue

rites.desc: Jingxue Confucians seek moral truth in the exact words of the ancient classics, holding that the sages' meaning is recovered through rigorous textual study rather than speculation.
rites.name: Jingxue

rites.desc: Donyi-Poloism is that main form of the Tani Lhoba religion that worships the dual Sun-Moon deities that are the eyes of the creator god Sedi as the Supreme Being.
rites.name: Donyi-Poloism

rites.desc: Sedism is a form of the Tani Lhoba religion that worships the creator god Sedi as the Supreme Being.
rites.name: Sedism

rites.desc: The revelations granted to Buddha, Zoroaster and Jesus were incomplete reflections of the real world. The prophet Mani brought the final revelation of the existence of the spiritual world of light and the material world of darkness, and how human souls, as with all light, gradually return to the creator.
rites.name: Manichaeism

rites.desc: According to the doctrine of Buddha Móní, the celestial Kingdom of Light is besieged by the Kingdom of Darkness, and all await the day that the Radiant Lord, to whom the sun and moon render their homage, will dispatch his messengers to the earth to spread enlightenment and liberate the people from their suffering.
rites.name: Mingism

rites.desc: Mandaeism traces its lineage to Adam, with John the Baptist as their greatest prophet. The world consists of light and darkness, and in time all mortal souls will be judged as to whether they are worthy to return to the eternal light.
rites.name: Mandaeism

rites.desc: Sabianism believes in the eternally existing God, and a material world created by Satan. They worship the angelic caretakers of the world, who — together with the Prophets — guide humanity towards heaven, and reunification with God.
rites.name: Sabianism

rites.desc: The Father, the original creator, is the depth of all knowledge, and the path to true understanding — gnosis. Achieving knowledge improves the world, and once the world is collectively lifted from its material ignorance, the world will return to its spiritual, natural state.
rites.name: Valentinianism

rites.desc: Caine was the first victim of the Evil of the Demiurge, creator of all physical matter. Since matter and bodies are evil, bodies must be defiled and destroyed through sinfulness, so that the true human soul within can be freed.
rites.name: Cainitism

rites.desc: There exists two kingdoms, one of Light and one of Darkness. Human souls were intended to conquer the Kingdom of Darkness, but fell and were trapped in the material realm. Among humans there were Twelve Patriarchs of Light who failed to overcome the Darkness, as they were split between body and soul. Thus God sent the Saviour to earth, and through his death once again enabled the freeing of human spirits.
rites.name: Priscillianism

rites.desc:
The Unknown God emanated all existence into the perfect Pleroma, filled by gracious eons, first among them Barbelo the Mother-Father.
A corruption caused the existence of Yaldabaoth, who stole a shred of divinity and created the material world. However, when he created mankind, he accidentally gave them his stolen spark of divinity. Yaldabaoth will spend eternity attempting to reclaim his power, while mankind must strive to return themselves to Barbelo and the Unknown God.
rites.name: Sethianism

rites.desc: In Vaishnavism, Vishnu is the Supreme Lord, and the most important devas are his many incarnated avatars, such as Rama and Krishna. Each of these various incarnations work to restore balance to the universe.
rites.name: Vaishnavism

rites.desc: Krishna is the authentic form of the Supreme Being, and Vishnu is his avatar when he takes form as the omnipotent. Through his divine avatars, he is present in all things.
rites.name: Krishnaism

rites.desc: Shaivites worship Shiva, the creator and destroyer of worlds, as the Supreme Being that exists in all things. In the same fashion as Shiva works to maintain balance and preserve the universe, the faithful must strive to bring balance into their lives.
rites.name: Shaivism

rites.desc: Unlike many Hindu faiths, Advaita Vedanta emphasizes the unity of the Atman, the true self, with the Brahman, the truest reality, and believes that moksha can be achieved in life as well as death.
rites.name: Advaita Vedanta

rites.desc: Shaktism believes in the Great Goddess as the Supreme Being from which springs all existence. The Srikula worship Tripura Sundari as the highest aspect of the Goddess, and the source of all Shakti, the energy of the universe.
rites.name: Srikula Shaktism

rites.desc: Shaktism believes in the Great Goddess as the Supreme Being from which springs all existence. The Kalikula worship Kali as the one who can give guidance, good rebirth and ultimately moksha.
rites.name: Kalikula Shaktism

rites.desc: The Smarta tradition rejects the worship of individual gods. Brahman is one and eternal, and Vishnu, Devi, Shiva, Ganesh and Surya are worshiped as equal avatars of the Supreme Being. Any individual worship is a step towards achieving understanding and unity with Brahman.
rites.name: Smartism

rites.desc: Surya the Sun God, the visible Brahman, is the foremost deity of the Saurites. Rooted in Vedic tradition, Saurites characterize Surya as being seated in a chariot drawn by seven horses, each one representing a color of the rainbow.
rites.name: Saurism

rites.desc: As explicitly stated in the Holy Qur'an, Nabi means being chosen by the Almighty to deliver His message and to remind people of the Day when they will be summoned before Him and held accountable for their actions. According to the core belief, Prophet Muhammad was the last of them.
rites.name: Nabi

rites.desc: Developed from the teachings of the jurist and theologian Abu Hanifa, who systemised the use of reasoning. Hanafi legal theory primarily derives law from the Quran, the Sunnah, scholarly consensus and analogical reasoning.
rites.name: Hanafi

rites.desc: The Hanbali school is the smallest of the four major Sunni Islamic jurisprudence schools, based on Ahmad ibn Hanbal's teachings. Unlike others, Hanbalis oppose codifying law into a comprehensive system, emphasising the Qur'an and Hadith as the highest sources.
rites.name: Hanbali

rites.desc: One of the four major schools of Islamic jurisprudence within Sunni Islam. It was founded by Malik ibn Anas in the 8th century. The Maliki school differs from the other Sunni schools of law most notably in the sources it uses for derivation of rulings.
rites.name: Maliki

rites.desc: Also known as the Companions of Muhammad, they were Muslim followers who met or saw him during his lifetime. The companions played a significant role in the early Muslim struggle, society, hadith narration, and governance.
rites.name: Sahabah

rites.desc: The school of al-Shafi'i, the Muslim scholar and jurist of the early 9th century known as 'the father of Muslim jurisprudence'. The core of Shafi'i thought: each act of a believer under the Law answers to a statute in the Revealed Law, the Shari'a.
rites.name: Shafi'i

rites.desc: Described as the generation of Muslims who followed the companions (Sahabah) of Prophet Muhammad, and thus received their teachings secondhand before the arrival of Sunni schools in later centuries.
rites.name: Tabi'un

rites.desc: A Shia rite that considers the line of true Imams — those imbued with divine knowledge and infallibility — to run through Isma'il bin Jafar. They are also known as Seveners, as Isma'il was the seventh Imam after Muhammad.
rites.name: Isma'ilism

rites.desc: Alawite religious teachings are secretive, and the Quran is only one of their sacred texts. In addition to the belief in the succession of Imams through Ali, Alawis also believe in reincarnation, and that all beings were stars cast out of heaven who must now re-earn their place by living successive good and faithful lives.
rites.name: Alawism

rites.desc: Alevis believe in the succession of the Twelve Imams, but also follow many other traditions as outlined in their collection of holy texts, the Buyruks. In Alevi tradition, God is the Truth, and Muhammad and Ali are manifestations of Him in the world.
rites.name: Alevism

rites.desc: Hafizis put precedence on supporting who they consider to be the true caliph above all others, as well as resisting any and all attempts to unseat or depose them. In defeat, they are defined by rebellion for a worthy cause, and in victory, proud adherence to the will of their leader.
rites.name: Hafizi

rites.desc: Ikhtilafis believe in the divine nature of the infallible Imams, starting with Ali. God has not only appointed and inspired them, but partially inhabits them to guide their acts, and by extension all of the Ummah.
rites.name: Ikhtilafism

rites.desc: Imamis believe that Twelve Imams were prophesied to lead the Ummah, and that the twelfth Imam, Imam Zaman, is waiting to return to lead Muslims into the Day of Judgement.
rites.name: Imamism

rites.desc: A rationalist rite that emphasizes reasoning in interpretation of the Quran and hadiths. Being Imam is hereditary, and they trace the line of succession to Ali.
rites.name: Nizarism

rites.desc: A true Imam is not infallible, but defined by their struggle against corruption and evil. Zayidis are therefore defined by their belief that Zayd ibn Ali was the rightful successor to the Imamate, due to his rebellion against the Umayyads.
rites.name: Zayidism

rites.desc: The Muhakkima believe the Islamic community doesn't need a Caliph or Imam if no suitable candidate exists. They reject the line of Ali and Abu Bakr's successors as inherently worthy leaders, emphasizing righteous conduct and consensus.
rites.name: Muhakkima

rites.desc: Recognizing no worthy successor to Muhammad, the Azariqas consider it their right and duty to struggle against any leader who does not uphold the values of their faith. Indeed, any difference in interpretation of faith would mark one as an infidel.
rites.name: Azraqism

rites.desc: Adherents of the Najdati branch of the Khawarij firmly believe in the establishment of Muslim leadership through the consensus of the faithful. The leader is not infallible, but through the community they are chosen by God.
rites.name: Najdatism

rites.desc: The Sufri believe in divine guidance and leadership through the interpretation of the word of God, rather than inheritance. The will of God becomes known as an expression of the Ummah's will, as long as the people of the Ummah are well-versed in the Quran.
rites.name: Sufrism

rites.desc: A reformist branch of Sunni Islam that originated with the Berber tribes in northern Africa, the Almohadi movement saw themselves as unitarians and preached a doctrine of purified monotheism.
rites.name: Almohadism

rites.desc: A literalist interpretation of Islam that emphasizes that the Quran as the only source of divine wisdom, and should be followed to the letter, ignoring hadith and fatwas.
rites.name: Quranism

rites.desc: Hailing from the Mountain of Druze, the Druze faith follows many of the principles of Isma'ilism, but also includes gnostic beliefs in an esoteric theology focused on the Truth of existence.
rites.name: Druze

rites.desc: A branch of Isma'ilism that incorporated elements of Zoroastrianism. The number of Imams was preordained by God to be seven, and there could therefore be no more Imams before the seventh Imam — Muhammad ibn Isma'il — returned to guide the faithful.
rites.name: Qarmatianism

rites.desc: Kevala Jnana frees the body from all physical needs. However, the soul can only be freed when completely naked, which is why Digambara monks must live without clothes.
rites.name: Digambara

rites.desc: Kevala Jnana is a state of the soul, not of ones physical being. Through good lives, one can achieve omniscience and leave the endless cycle. The moment of moksha itself is only achievable through death, when one becomes Siddha.
rites.name: Svetambara

rites.desc: The faith of Yapaniya Jains has some similarity to both the Svetambara and Digambara traditions, provoking the faithful of both faiths. Yapaniya mendicants are expected to be naked, much like Digambaran ones, but they do not adhere to their strict rules. The faith also holds that women can attain Moksha and nuns are common within the faith.
rites.name: Yapaniya

rites.desc: Rabbinism emphasizes the rabbis' purpose as interpreters of the religious law of the Halakha. Laws and traditions is what ensures the covenant with the Lord is kept, and the rabbis guard those laws.
rites.name: Rabbinism

rites.desc: Merkabah Mysticism is a sect of Judaic mysticism sharing some influence from Gnostic teachings. The faith is centered on visions, adopting ascetic lifestyles to join the Throne of God.
rites.name: Merkabah

rites.desc: In the matters of religious law, the Tanakh alone is the highest and absolute authority. The role of rabbis are not to reassess and adapt the rules of the covenant, but to interpret their literal meaning.
rites.name: Karaism

rites.desc: The rabbis, or kahen, judge in matters of religious law, but they work together with a circle of elders who judge in matters of tradition and life.
rites.name: Haymanot

rites.desc: As the descendants of the tribes of Israel spread across the world, they built smaller communities from west to east, acting as tribes of their own. Also called Cochin Jews, they made their new home in the Cochin Kingdom of South India. There, they intermixed with the local people and exchanged cultures.
rites.name: Malabarism

rites.desc: Descended from the tribes that settled Samaria, Samaritans follow an original, unchanged version of the Torah. In this way they are practicing the true religion of Moses, serving the direct duties granted by God.
rites.name: Samaritanism

rites.desc: A community of converts, Kuzarites follow the common Rabbinic interpretation of the Halakha. Even long after their conversion, they continue to hold some local beliefs and traditions with religious reverence.
rites.name: Kuzarism

rites.desc: A spirit-medium faith in which shamans host gods and ancestral spirits during Gut rituals to heal, divine, and restore harmony for households and villages.
rites.name: Mu

rites.desc: Kiratism is the practice of Mundhism that is common between a majority of the Kirati people. It focuses on the worship of Tagera Ningwaphuma as the Supreme Being and the honoring of ancestors.
rites.name: Kiratism

rites.desc: Yumaites focus their worship on Yuma Sammang, the female personification of Tagera Ningwaphuma, as the Supreme Goddess, whom they hail as the Mother of Nature.
rites.name: Yumaism

rites.desc: The religion of the Rrmea, or Qiang, focus much of their worship on the veneration of white stones, or Vvluphi. Shaman-priests known as xbi wear a monkey fur hat and beat a sheep-skin drum while performing rituals.
rites.name: Vvluphixje

rites.desc: The indigenous beliefs of the Tangut people focused around the White Crane being the heavenly male aspect of the divine, while the Red Monkey was seen as the earthly female aspect of divinity, and non-Buddhist Tangut society was divided into two classes along these principles: the priestly 'Black-headed' and the 'Red-faced' commoners.
rites.name: Melie

rites.desc: The spiritual world is all around us, and spirits inhabit all parts of the world. Anything can be inhabited by the supernatural — a bed, a mountain, even a rainstorm. It is important to maintain harmony with this spiritual world, and give it due respect and recognition.
rites.name: Shintō

rites.desc: The way to spiritual power is through discipline. To understand the spiritual world, followers of Shugendō observe a multitude of rituals, and seek out the most sacred spaces where the wall between the human world and the spiritual world is at its thinnest.
rites.name: Shugendō

rites.desc: Shangqing Taoism was the dominant form of Taoism during the Tang Dynasty. Its followers seek to harmonize themselves with the universe through mediation and physical exercises, as opposed to the talismans and alchemy used by other branches of Taoism.
rites.name: Shangqing

rites.desc: Followers of Quanzhen Taoism practice internal alchemy to perfect their bodies and harmonize themselves with the Tao. Through this process practitioners achieve physical longevity and spiritual immortality.
rites.name: Quanzhen

rites.desc: Unlike the other Taoist schools, Zhengyis observe a strict theocratic hierarchy under the Celestial Master. Practitioners craft and sell protective talismans to prevent the loss of qi, the life energy which sustains all living things.
rites.name: Zhengyi

rites.desc: The world is ruled by many deities, but they are all subject to the highest one, Waaq, the god of the sky. Rain and life is brought down to us from above.
rites.name: Waaqism

rites.desc: The world is ruled by the High God, Ngai, but our ancestors intervene in our affairs and merit their own propriations. Under the greatest trees of the land, we beseech and praise them all.
rites.name: Gothaithaya Ngai

rites.desc: Emphasizing harmony and balance, adherents of this native Mandé faith revere the twin offspring of Amma, known together as the Nummo, who were seen as two parts of one complete, perfect being.
rites.name: Siguism

rites.desc: Adherents of this native Soninke faith worship the serpent-deity Bida, a capricious entity who demands regular sacrifices but rewards followers with blessings and bountiful harvests.
rites.name: Bidaism

rites.desc: The Yazidi believe that God created the world and placed it under the protection of seven angels, foremost among them Tawûsê Melek, the Peacock Angel. The Peacock Angel at first fell from God's grace, but his tears of remorse extinguished the fires of his prison, and he was reunited with God. In the same manner, we all seek to reunite with God at the end of many long lifetimes.
rites.name: Yazidism

rites.desc: Followers of the Book of Revelation, which tells of Xwedê's greatness.
rites.name: Kitêbacilweism

rites.desc: Followers of the Black Book, which describes how the Lord came down from Black Mountain and created the world.
rites.name: Meshefaresism

rites.desc: Humans aid in the struggle against Aka Manah through good thoughts and lives. This is done through ritual purity, the preservation of nature and the destruction of evil creatures.
rites.name: Mazdayasna

rites.desc: Followers of the teachings of Behafarid, Behafaridites seek cooperation with the Islamic world, making numerous reforms to their faith in response to Muslim criticisms of mainline Zoroastrianism. Among these reforms are banning the consumption of alcohol, strict opposition to familial marriage, and encouraging charity as a measure of using one's wealth for public good.
rites.name: Behafaridism

rites.desc: Based on the idea that Ahura Mazda, through his thoughts, created evil spirits by accident, Gayomarthians reject the infabillity of the Lord of Wisdom, and instead emphasize ritualistic practice to learn Truth in communion with Ahura Mazda.
rites.name: Gayomartianism

rites.desc: With deep roots in the religious admixture of Sogdiana, the Khurmazta worship a wide set of gods and spirits, both ancestral and universal. They also revere icons, something anathema to many other Zoroastrians. Yet as unique as some aspects of their faith may be, in other ways they remain within the orbit of mainstream Zoroastrian doctrine, practicing the purity rituals and tending the eternal fires with unceasing devotion.
rites.name: Khurmazdism

rites.desc: The radical prophets Zardusht Khuragan and Mazdak were influenced by esoteric faiths of late antiquity, and agitated for shared ownership of resources and universal cooperation between humans to overcome the five demons of avarice, wrath, envy, possessiveness and vengeance.
rites.name: Mazdakism

rites.desc: In a world of Light and Darkness, unjust rulers must be overthrown in support of what is good. Through prophets such as Mazdak, Abu Muslim and al-Muqanna, Khurramites believe that the divine is born into humanity, and will one day return to lead them as the Messiah.
rites.name: Khurramism

rites.desc: Many ancient beliefs still resonate in the Arewordik faith, a sect of cryptic Zoroastrians with Ohrmazd (as Aramazd) ruling over a pantheon of gods, including the Sun itself, that together direct the world.
rites.name: Arewordik

rites.desc: Steeped in Daylamite traditions as well as Persian paganism, many aspects of Afridunism predate even the ancient Zoroastrian creed. Adherents strive to live according to the rules laid down by the mythical hero Faridun, which emphasizes the absolute power of family leaders and a fierce spirit of independence.
rites.name: Afridunism
